quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by an /l/?
quests.textToSpeak: could we get another bottle of water
quests.hint: Your tongue tip stays up for /l/. Which word ends that way before a vowel?
quests.explanation: With 'bottle of', the tongue stays raised for the /l/ as the weak /əv/ begins. 'Get another' links through /t/. Ordering is usually said fast, so the weak 'of' is nearly invisible.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Which connection comes first in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: I'll have the soup and a salad
quests.hint: Say the sentence at normal speed and mark each place where a consonant runs into a vowel. Take the first.
quests.explanation: 'And' shrinks to /ən/ in a food order, so the /p/ of 'soup' lands straight on it and the two sound like one word. 'And a' follows as a second link, and together they make an easy rhythm for the order.
quests.flowRule: Reduced forms: Unstressed to, and, of, at, it, us and a shrink to /tə/, /ən/, /əv/, /ət/, /ɪt/, /əs/ and /ə/, so a link into one of them sounds like the end of the word before it.

quests.instruction: Which link has a nasal sound meeting a vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: would you like a drink or anything else
quests.hint: Only a few word endings use the nose. Find one that is followed by a vowel sound.
quests.explanation: The nasal of 'anything' runs into the opening vowel of 'else', so the end of the question is one smooth run. 'Like a' and 'drink or' link through /k/. Servers say this on repeat, so the whole line is smoothed into a few beats.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a nasal sound?
quests.textToSpeak: I'd like to make an appointment
quests.hint: Skip the stops and hisses. Which boundary has a nasal on the left and a vowel on the right?
quests.explanation: 'An' ends in /n/ and 'appointment' begins with the weak /ə/, so the voice keeps humming across the boundary. 'Make an' links through /k/. A booking request is polite and quick, so the links do not get pauses.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which is the last connection in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: I've had a headache all day
quests.hint: Several boundaries link, but only one comes last. Which?
quests.explanation: A /k/ at the end of 'headache' is released into the /ɔː/ of 'all' rather than being held. 'Had a' comes earlier. Symptoms are described in one breath, so this link is usually unbroken.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which link closes the sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: take one tablet at a time
quests.hint: Read left to right and take the final link.
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'at' goes straight onto the weak /ə/ of 'a', so the pair becomes one short beat, and 'tablet at' sits just before it. Instructions on a label are often read in this reduced way.
quests.flowRule: Reduced forms: Unstressed to, and, of, at, it, us and a shrink to /tə/, /ən/, /əv/, /ət/, /ɪt/, /əs/ and /ə/, so a link into one of them sounds like the end of the word before it.

quests.instruction: Which link is released from a stop (p, t, k, b, d or g)?
quests.textToSpeak: could I speak to someone in accounts
quests.hint: Look for a puff (p, t, k) or a voiced release (b, d, g) right before a vowel.
quests.explanation: Because 'could' is usually weak, its /d/ is released straight into the /aɪ/ of 'I', so you hear one beat. 'Someone in' and 'in accounts' link through /n/. Phone requests are said fast, so the first link is often the clearest.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which link begins with a stop sound?
quests.textToSpeak: I'm calling about an order
quests.hint: One word ends with the mouth closed, then opens straight into the next word's vowel. Which?
quests.explanation: Listen for the /t/ of 'about' sliding onto the weak /ən/. 'Calling about' and 'an order' link through nasals, so they are different in kind. This is a standard way to open a call.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Count the links from the start: find the second one
quests.textToSpeak: let me check if it's in stock
quests.hint: Count the links from the start and stop at two.
quests.explanation: 'If' ends in /f/ and 'it's' begins with /ɪ/, so the hiss runs on. 'Check if' comes first and 'it's in' last, so together they form a continuous chain of linked sound. Someone checking stock speaks quickly.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which link do you hear first?
quests.textToSpeak: please hand it in before Friday
quests.hint: A short chain of two links. Take the first.
quests.explanation: Three words run together in this instruction. The /d/ of 'hand' lands on the vowel of 'it', and 'it in' follows, so the whole chunk is one smooth run.
quests.flowRule: Chained links: In phrases like verb + it + particle, each word connects to the next, so one consonant lands on a vowel and the following consonant lands on the next vowel in one flowing line.

quests.instruction: Find the link that runs on a hum (m, n or ng)
quests.textToSpeak: this exam starts at ten o'clock
quests.hint: Think of /m/, /n/ and /ŋ/. Which of them ends a word and meets a vowel?
quests.explanation: 'Ten' ends in /n/ and 'o'clock' begins with the weak /ə/, so the voice runs straight on and the time sounds like a single word. 'This exam' and 'starts at' link through /s/ instead, which you can hold, so they are different in kind.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by a 'ch' or 'j' sound
quests.textToSpeak: please highlight each answer
quests.hint: Say the candidates slowly: only one ends in a 'ch' or 'j' sound and is followed by a vowel.
quests.explanation: The 'ch' sound at the end of 'each' is released straight into 'answer'. 'Highlight each' links through /t/. A teacher giving an instruction usually speaks at a steady pace without breaks.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by the sound /l/
quests.textToSpeak: pass it on and tell everyone
quests.hint: A long sentence with several links. Which one is carried by /l/?
quests.explanation: Dark /l/ plus a vowel makes the link in 'tell everyone': the tongue stays up as the vowel starts. 'Pass it on and' is a chain of links before it, which makes the whole sentence run on.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Which link is carried by a buzz or a hiss?
quests.textToSpeak: shut it off and unplug it
quests.hint: A hiss or a buzz you can hold. Which word ends in one before a vowel?
quests.explanation: 'Off' ends in /f/, which you can sustain, and 'and' is weak /ən/, so the airflow keeps going. Most of the other links use stops, so this is the only held-sound link.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which pair links even though the first word ends in a silent e?
quests.textToSpeak: just take it easy tonight
quests.hint: One word is spelled with a final e that you never say. Which pair does it start?
quests.explanation: Despite its spelling, 'take' ends in /k/, and that /k/ lands on 'it'. Then 'it easy' follows. A friendly line like this works because nothing interrupts it.
quests.flowRule: Linking follows sound, not spelling: a silent final 'e' (as in 'give' or 'close') does not block a link, because the word really ends in a consonant sound such as /v/ or /z/.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a 'ch' or 'j' sound?
quests.textToSpeak: switch it off and open a window
quests.hint: The tongue releases with a brief hiss at the end of one word, straight into a vowel. Which?
quests.explanation: A 'ch' at the end of 'switch' is released into the vowel of 'it'. The remaining links, 'it off', 'off and', 'and open' and 'open a', make a chain that carries the sentence to the end.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Which link has a nasal sound meeting a vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: hang up all the clothes
quests.hint: At normal speed, one boundary has no break at all, just a hum. Listen for it.
quests.explanation: The nasal at the end of 'hang' runs into the vowel of 'up' with the voice still on. 'Up all' links through /p/. Housework instructions are brisk, so the links run together.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a stop sound meets a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: the dog is always at the door
quests.hint: Find the boundary where a closure is released into a vowel instead of being held.
quests.explanation: 'Dog' ends in /g/ and 'is' begins with /ɪ/, so the /g/ releases into the vowel. 'Is always' and 'always at' are carried by /z/. A sentence like this is a good test of whether you can hear the first link before the sentence speeds up.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.textToSpeak: the file is in a shared folder

quests.explanation: 'File' ends in /l/ and 'is' begins with /ɪ/, so the tongue stays raised as the vowel starts. 'Is in' and 'in a' follow. This sentence rolls along because every word attaches to its neighbour.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.hint: 'I'll use' looks like it could link. Check how 'use' begins before you decide.
